Medium · Media and streaming

Video streaming

You run a movie and series service for a growing audience. Each viewer pulls a few seconds of video at a time for two hours straight. Bandwidth is the largest cost by far, and everyone wants to start watching in the evening. Practise this medium system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

Draw your design, run a full traffic day and see how it holds.

Play this problem

The brief

You run a movie and series service for a growing audience. Each viewer pulls a few seconds of video at a time for two hours straight. Bandwidth is the largest cost by far, and everyone wants to start watching in the evening.

Think of a video service like Netflix.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
400 thousand subscribers
Audience in plain numbers
400,000 users or devices
Normal peak
≈ 600 requests per second
Request mix
Stream chunk: 80%; Read: 10%; Search: 4%; Sign-in: 2%; Analytics event: 4%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Stream chunk: ≈ 1,000 ms; Read: ≈ 300 ms; Search: ≈ 400 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
At most 1 minute of writes may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $108,000
Data at rest
≈ 250 TB
Where users are
North America: 60%; Europe: 30%; Asia Pacific: 10%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Stream chunk: 900 seconds; Read: 900 seconds; Search: 900 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds; Analytics event: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • Each viewer fetches one 2 MB chunk every 4 seconds.
  • Bandwidth is priced per gigabyte sent to viewers (about 4 cents at list price, approx.).

Questions that shape the design

Is most of the library watched equally?

No. A few hundred titles get most of the viewing. The long tail is watched rarely.

How long can a viewer wait for the picture to start?

About a second for each chunk. More than that and the picture freezes.

Do viewers need to be signed in?

Yes. A subscription check happens once at the start, not for every chunk.

What if a new season launches?

A huge crowd presses play on the same episode in the same hour. It is the busiest night of the quarter.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 19:00 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic reaches 8 times the scheduled load; rises over 30 seconds, holds for 900 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds.

  2. 12:00 · Cache stampede

    The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

    Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

  3. 21:00 · Cost blowout

    A crawler hits uncached pages all day, and every pay-per-use part of the bill multiplies.

    Traffic for Read, Search reaches 1.5 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 21,600 seconds and eases over 600 seconds. Other request types keep their scheduled load. Billed usage multiplier: 3. Duration: ≈ 21,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • A few titles get most of the views. How can you use that to protect your storage and your bill?
  • Deliver versioned video segments while bounding cold-origin load and startup delay.
  • Every extra copy layer (edge, shield, storage) lowers your storage load, but each one adds a little delay for a rare title nobody has watched yet.
  • Serving fewer quality levels shrinks the bill but makes the picture worse on a fast connection.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Copies near users
  • Where the money goes
  • Hot, warm, cold and archive

Related problems

  • Easy

    Photo sharing

    You are building a photo app. People post pictures and everyone else scrolls through them. Almost all the traffic is people looking at photos, and the photos take up far more room than anything else you store.

  • Easy

    Podcast hosting

    You host shows for creators. Listeners press play and download big audio files, and creators upload a new episode now and then. The audio is the bill: every episode downloaded costs bandwidth.

  • Medium

    Disappearing stories

    People post photos and short clips that vanish after 24 hours. Followers tap through a tray of stories every day, and the poster sees who looked. Deleting on time matters: storage must not grow forever.

  • Medium

    Patch day downloads

    A popular game ships a 5 GB update at 10 am. Millions of players press Update within the same hour. The files are identical for everyone, so the work is moving huge amounts of data without a huge bill, while players still log in and play.
